Turning Turtles

Game StrategyPlace ValueInvariants
Game: Take turns with the computer turning an O into an X. Whoever turns the last O wins.
How to play: Click an O, and if you like a square to its left to flip as well (O to X or X to O), then press Make Move.

Look for the math

In the original version from Winning Ways, players turn turtles onto their backs and back onto their feet; here O and X stand in for them. The game is Nim in disguise.

Squares are heaps

Think of square k holding an O as a Nim heap of k counters, and an X as an empty heap. Turning the O at k empties that heap. If you also flip a square j to its left, the result counts as a heap of j in its place, whether square j was O or X before. So the move is "take k − j counters from heap k". Every Nim move appears this way, and nothing else does.

The Nim-sum

Write the numbers of the O squares in binary and add them without carrying: that is their Nim-sum, or XOR, s. If s = 0, every move makes it nonzero. If s ≠ 0, some O square k has k xor s < k: turn it and flip k xor s (no flip if that is 0), and the Nim-sum is 0 again. The player who keeps handing over Nim-sum 0 makes the last move. The logic test searched the whole game, all 2,048 rows, and confirmed that a row is lost for the player to move exactly when its Nim-sum is 0.

The computer

The computer plays the Nim move whenever it can and a random O otherwise. The original applet looked for its heap in a slightly different way, and in 9 of the 1,920 rows where it should win, that rule asked for a flip to the right, which the rules forbid. The computer here always plays a legal winning move. The test checked that from every winning row it wins against every reply.

Before each move, add up the O numbers in binary without carrying. Can you leave the computer a Nim-sum of 0?
